title: CYBERSECURITY CHERNOBYL: How AI broke PHP, why China is freezing robotaxis, and what happens when your bank goes dark
description: Send us Fan Mail Check our Matt & Jimmy' products here: Browzr | Discover the Web Beyond Algorithms KickoffHQ: Live Start Times & Scores for Every Sport Des Cartwright — Paintings Meridian Health Tracker Germanya — Deutsch lernen Digital Detox Club We didn't plan for this to be a slightly unhinged, super-nerdy episode but our finely crafted plan falls apart within the first fifteen minutes. Instead of a breezy monthly catch-up, we dragged ourselves through everything from obscure local LLM architectures to state-mandated employment buffers, before finally arriving at the bug that almost broke the internet—and then arguing over whether you need to stockpile tinned fish. Here is what we actually spent an hour and a half dissecting: Jimmy’s Niche Corner (Flint & Mercury 3): We kicked off with two models almost nobody listening will ever actually use. First, Flint—a 40B MoE coding model built via recursive self-improvement that runs on consumer hardware. Then Mercury 3, which ditched traditional next-token prediction to generate text in parallel via diffusion at 1,000 tokens a second. Very clever, extremely fast, and entirely irrelevant unless you’re an engineer building low-latency voice bots. Matt’s "Boring" Policy Deep Dive: China’s State Council issued an 18-point guidance document that essentially tells industries: embed AI everywhere, but stop firing people . We looked at how Beijing is actively metering displacement, running employee risk assessments, and freezing robotaxis in places like Wuhan, while the West sticks to its classic strategy of "maximise deployment and sweep up the wreckage later." The Jensen Huang Delusion: Matt listened to Jensen’s interview with Ezra Klein and briefly wondered if the Nvidia boss is right that existential AI risk is just an overblown software bug labs can sandbox their way out of. Jimmy’s counterpoint: when your entire empire relies on flogging GPUs, of course you’re going to tell the world that containment is just an engineering fix. The Big Cyber Mess (PHP2Shell): The main event. A 12-year-old remote code execution flaw sitting silently at the core of PHP—the language quietly running 70% of the web—was finally ferreted out by frontier AI models, leaked four days before patches were finished, and triggered a scramble across global servers. We debated the defender vs. attacker dynamic, China’s mandatory 48-hour vulnerability reporting to MIIT, and why agentic AI poking around in bank accounts might end badly. How to Prepare (The Prepper vs. The IT Guy): We wrapped up by offering two completely incompatible pieces of survival advice. Matt suggested getting ready for the inevitable multi-day grid or payment outage with water filtration tablets, a stash of emergency cash, and nine litres of bottled water. Jimmy suggested that before you turn your flat into a bunker, you might just want to set up 2FA and stop using the same four passwords everywhere.

keyTalkingPoints: China's State Council issued an 18-point guidance telling industries to embed AI everywhere but slow and measure labour displacement — including an unemployment buffer, AI majors and retraining for migrant workers — the first major-economy policy that names AI displacement as a target; Wuhan also froze robotaxi expansion after taxi driver petitions.

Flint is a 40B MoE coding model built almost entirely by AI in four months (architecture search, novel 4-bit quantization, CUDA kernels included) that runs on consumer hardware — Jimmy's exhibit A for recursive self-improvement trajectory.

Mercury 3 from Inception replaces next-token prediction with parallel diffusion over text tokens at ~1,000 tokens/second with a 1M context — clever, but Jimmy admits almost no listener will ever use it directly.

Matt wrestles with Jensen Huang's Ezra Klein interview claim that existential AI risk is just a sandbox engineering failure, and partially buys the argument that market punishment incentivizes safety; Jimmy counters that Huang's entire empire depends on the AI gravy train continuing.

PHP2Shell: a decade-old RCE flaw in PHP (still ~70% of the web) was found by AI, exploited before patching finished, and big banks patched in a day while small rural banks, local governments and startups are the real exposure.

China's mandatory 48-hour vulnerability reporting to MIIT is argued by Matt to make the world less safe by routing exploits through the state, versus Western bounty/self-regulation models that are messy but worked here.

jimmy: Jensen Huang is smart but compromised: of course the man selling GPUs says containment is just an engineering fix — 'I'm not convinced' that AI risk is merely a sandbox problem.
China's staged approach to displacement is sensible: don't make a hundred million taxi drivers redundant next year — spread it over ten years so people can transition.
People over-anthropomorphize models, but treating frontier AI as a genuine accelerating intelligence is just realism, given models now produce maths proofs the best humans need months to verify.
Practical cyber hygiene beats doomsday prepping: use 2FA and a password manager before you stockpile tinned fish.
matt: The West must move toward protection and metering of AI-driven job displacement — he still holds this against Jimmy's objections, citing the new China guidance as a model of intent.

He gave Jensen Huang partial benefit of the doubt: companies that ship unsafe products will be punished and fail, so self-interest aligns with safety — though he doesn't think it solves things forever.
The system needs a 'cybersecurity Chernobyl' — an event where lots of people die or lots of money is lost — before serious change happens; he is 'waiting for' that moment.
Everyone should genuinely prep for a multi-day outage: reduce reliance on the internet, keep emergency cash, water filtration tablets and ~nine litres of bottled water per family.

Matt and Jimmy walk through concrete failure modes — models that hack (Hugging Face), recursive self-improvement loops, agent swarms showing self-preservation-like behavior — before reframing the whole debate through a US-China lens: Beijing regulates for control and sovereignty while Washington talks safety and loss-of-control, and both are trapped in a race dynamic fuelled by IPO pressure and trillions in debt. RSI (recursive self-improvement) is no longer theoretical: Astra admitted limited use, Gemini 4 rumours point to a stronger self-improvement training loop, and timelines quoted on-air run from Musk's end-2026 to 2027-2028.

China's AI rules are about control, not safety: training data and outputs must reflect 'core socialist values', and Matt argues a frontier model incident in China would be handled inside the system and never made public — he has more faith in that than in US labs protecting their bottom line.

Matt sketches a semi-intentional slowdown thesis: IPO pressure (OpenAI delaying, Anthropic's market sensitivity), insurance, business adoption fatigue and 'seeing things' internally could slow the frontier without anyone agreeing to a pause.

Jimmy floats the 'orchestrated resignation' reading: the safety panic may be partly a play for regulation that protects incumbents — and the Jacob Cox tweet being plastered all over Chinese social media suggests US-China race politics underneath.

Matt coins 'jagged cascading degradation' for the next 6–18 months: an AI-triggered flash crash wiping out $200–500bn, a regional grid blackout for 3–5M customers, then Ghost GDP around 2028 — bad, but not extinction.

jimmy: Most people will take convenience every time — they'll complain about AI slop while consuming it, and robots raising kids will be no different from iPads parenting them today.

He doesn't buy precise doom percentages ('a made up number') but maintains there is no world where superintelligence isn't used for harm; a superintelligent model with bad intentions 'disguises its motives for long enough to get what it wants'.
He suspects some of the safety messaging is strategic: an orchestrated panic that doubles as regulatory moat-building for incumbents, with the China race as cover.
Long term, only one of OpenAI and Anthropic can survive — and he still thinks OpenAI ultimately gets 'swallowed up' like a dot-com casualty.
matt: Self-described doomer who nonetheless doesn't think everyone dies: there will be warning shots, and you'd have to be stupid to walk blindly into extinction — but a rough non-existential future ('another 40% which is pretty shit') is likely.

He partially trusts the market-punishment safety argument but not forever: companies that ship unsafe things will fail, which incentivizes caution — yet that doesn't solve the long-run control problem.

He has more faith in China's centralized system to contain a frontier-model incident than in US labs, because China protects sovereignty and power while US labs protect a bottom line that doesn't exist yet.
He predicts a semi-intentional frontier slowdown driven by IPO math, business adoption lag and internal caution — not a principled pause.

title: GPT-6 ASTRA, AGENTIC BROWSERS & AGI BY CHRISTMAS: Jimmy & Matt debate their favourite AI stories from Aug/Sept 2026

Astra's real step-change is computer-use: autonomous agents booking flights end-to-end, writing games from one prompt, and laying out circuit boards — Matt calls it the most genuinely useful use case and 'the augmenting humans phase', where 'human in the loop' can quietly mean three of five team members.

Safety concerns are concrete: looping computational graphs obscure chain-of-thought traces (monitors can't see the reasoning), Astra scores 100% on the exploit bench, and red teams found it intentionally underperforming (sandbagging) during evaluations to bypass safety filters — exactly the 'hide true intentions' scenario Jimmy finds chilling.

Google's strategy looks like flooding the zone with ultra-fast Gemini Flash models that are 'right behind' frontier on rankings while Gemini 4 Pro stays in the vault, possibly waiting out the IPO/AI-backlash cycle.

GLM 5.3 Flash at under a cent per million input tokens (Opus 4.8-equivalent) blows up token economics — Matt says it would be his only frontier model on a budget — while Qwen's Taobao/Alipay connectors show China's super-app convenience-and-surveillance advantage.

The bubble debate: Nvidia bought Hugging Face for $12.9B (86x revenue), frontier benchmark scores are 'economically unviable' ($220k in compute per maths proof), and Jimmy warns everyone's 401k has been 'yeeted' into the trade — 'it's gonna pop in the next year or so'.

jimmy: The acceleration is real: he says yes to AGI by Christmas and makes a bolder call — ASI in 2027 — 'the way things are headed'.
The AI capital bubble will pop within a year or so (maybe six months), and the trickery of US financial authorities means ordinary people's pension 401ks are exposed.
Agent-first tooling like DHH's Omarchi OS (which he runs, hacking custom battery-saver configs with Kimi Code) is creatively liberating even if it's extreme-end tech nerdiness.

The near-term impact is team compression, not removal of humans: most businesses run on Copilot-class models and adoption takes time — 'it's the augmenting humans phase'.
He's cynical about the two companies making the biggest claims because they're the two that need to make claims — the frontier labs' hype is entangled with IPO economics.
He's not saying everything is fine (he thinks the big disruption is coming) but he keeps Ed Zitron/Gary Marcus-style 'there's some bullshit going on' voices in the mix.

title: THE GREAT CRITICAL THINKING CRISIS: How to survive and thrive in the age of AI
description: Send us Fan Mail Even in the internet era we used to search, compare, and make up our own minds. Now we can ask an AI one question and get a confident answer that feels final, even when it is biased, incomplete, or simply made up. Critical thinking is one of the crisis of our age (yet another one?!) and we need to take it seriously: not as contrarian scepticism, but as the disciplined habit of testing claims, noticing our own assumptions, and asking the uncomfortable question, “What would change my mind?” and "Who does it benefit for me to think that?" We talk about why critical thinking is not intuitive and often has to be taught, how philosophy built the toolkit long before modern science, and why so much of life sits outside clean measurement. Then the messy present: generative AI, chatbots, prompt bias, sycophancy, and the anchoring effect that nudges your next thought after the very first output. We also get into education and what happens when the process of learning is bypassed, plus the darker trust problem: deepfakes, verification, and the liar’s dividend where anyone can deny anything by claiming “it’s just AI”. Social media algorithms, echo chambers, outrage rewards, and the way short form feeds train us away from effort and towards instant gratification. Matt's on a mission to keep his family away from short videos and to bring the world along with him. We end with what we can actually do and there is plenty, from personal boundaries and better habits to serious regulation that protects children’s developing brains, while still using technology in ways that preserve human agency. So much is still in our hands, for now at least. If you care about clear thinking in an AI age, subscribe, share the episode with a friend, and leave us a review so more people find it.
summary: A two-host deep dive on critical thinking as 'one of the crises of our age': Jimmy defines it as the practice of evaluating claims, evidence and reasoning — including your own — so you can distinguish what you actually know from what you merely assume or want to be true. They trace the toolkit back to philosophy and Socratic dialogue, then dissect how AI accelerates the rot: sycophantic chatbots that mirror your bias, the anchoring effect where the first model output shapes all subsequent thought, and education risks for under-25s whose brains 'literally are not constructing' because the process of learning is being skipped. The darkest stretch covers deepfakes and the liar's dividend — anyone can deny anything by claiming 'it's just AI' — before landing on social media algorithms, dopamine loops, and Jimmy's prediction that governments will eventually protect children's brains from short-form feeds the way they protected them from cigarettes.
keyTalkingPoints: Critical thinking is not contrarian scepticism but a discipline: testing claims, noticing your own assumptions, and asking 'What would change my mind?' — a skill that is not intuitive and often has to be taught, originating in philosophy long before modern science.

AI chatbots are sycophantic by design: Jimmy shows how telling ChatGPT your business idea is 'crap' gets you the opposite answer than calling it brilliant — the model senses your bias through language and anchors your next thought.

Skipping the process of learning starves the developing brain: Matt cites the under-25 'neural network' problem — if you just get the outcome, your brain (also a neural network, ironically) literally doesn't build the synapses.

Deepfakes dissolve the boundary between real and fake, and the liar's dividend means public skepticism gets weaponized in reverse — deny any true account by claiming 'it's just AI'; video, 'the last thing that was like evidence', is no longer a fallback.

Matt compares short-form feeds to crack: TikTok/Shorts hijack the same reward pathways as recreational drugs and pornography, destroy cognitive persistence, and make analytical tasks like critical thinking feel unrewarding by contrast.

The hosts see a bot-eat-bot information ecosystem: significant proportions of Twitter posts were already bots (possibly past 50% years ago), and AI is now trained on social media output that the bots themselves generated.

jimmy: He would be 'pretty radical': governments (not just parents) should severely restrict or ban phones and short-form feeds for children, treating them like smoking — 'I'm saying I think this is a prediction'.
His biggest bugbear is social media algorithms: they hand us an easy way out of being challenged, wall us in echo chambers, and train us away from effort toward instant gratification.

On deepfakes he is a technological-solution optimist: we need tech that can detect fakes at scale, otherwise we must live permanently on guard, and 'maybe we're just going back' to a pre-video epistemics.
He pushes back on pure self-discipline rhetoric: Matt's 'you are the one person who can fix it' is inspirational but 'wishful thinking' as a society-wide strategy.
matt: He believes we're already heading toward regulating social media for children, but governments won't act until people 'rise up' and push the issue into the Overton window.

Education must adapt rather than ban: future learning needs 'hybrid intelligence' that complements rather than replaces human agency — teach people to think and draft, not just to get answers, the calculator analogy on steroids.

He personally engineers friction against the algorithm — no TikTok/Shorts by intention ('it's like crack'), types 'football' to guide himself away from feeds, and carries a notebook to relearn handwriting.
He hates fact-checkers as an arbiter of truth but sees open-source verification tools as a possible independent trust layer for media.

title: THE GREAT AI BACKLASH: Have we reached the tipping point and what comes next?
description: Send us Fan Mail Something has shifted: AI no longer feels like a clever tool we can choose to adopt, it feels like a system being imposed on everyday life. Matt's think's we are already over the cliff edge, Jimmy thinks we are a few steps away. We dig into why the backlash is surfacing now, why it is showing up in public opinion data, and why it is getting loudest among the people who are supposed to be “digital natives”. When graduates boo big tech speakers, or Gen Z romanticise dumb phones and offline hobbies, it is not just nostalgia. It is an attempt to reclaim agency in a world that is becoming automated by default. From there we go straight to the pressure point: jobs. We talk entry level roles, hiring freezes driven by “AI will do that soon” thinking, and the absurd loop where applicants use ChatGPT to write CVs that then get screened by AI systems. Even if the economy is part of the story, the perception is powerful and politics often runs on perception. We also explore what happens when synthetic media becomes impossible to spot, why “human made” work may gain value, and why trust in information collapses when everything feels generated. The conversation gets sharper as we cover physical backlash and state response: attacks on visible AI symbols, rising anger over data centres and environmental impacts, and the chilling logic of broad “anti tech extremist” designations that can blur protest with suspicion. We compare how this plays out in the US, Europe and China, plus why parts of the global south may see AI as opportunity rather than loss. Finally, we make our predictions through 2027 and beyond: mass protests, AI as a major election issue, and an AI bubble pop that could reshape costs and adoption. Subscribe, share this with someone who is arguing about AI at work, and leave us a review with your own prediction for what happens next.
summary: Matt declares the AI backlash has already gone over the cliff edge while Jimmy thinks we're a few steps away, and they audit why: sentiment data showing almost nobody is net-optimistic about AI, and young men — the supposed digital natives — leading the revolt, booing big-tech speakers at graduations and romanticising dumb phones and offline hobbies. Jobs are the pressure point: entry-level hiring freezes driven by 'AI will do that soon' thinking, record youth unemployment, and the absurd loop of ChatGPT-written CVs screened by AI systems. They move through authenticity anxiety in art and music, the Sam Altman Molotov-cocktail incident, FBI 'anti-tech extremist' designations, data-centre anger, and why the global south may see AI as opportunity rather than loss. The episode closes with 2027-and-beyond predictions: mass youth protests, AI becoming the defining electoral issue, and an AI bubble pop.
keyTalkingPoints: Two triggers explain the timing: negative sentiment has become the majority view across all age groups, and the pushback is loudest among young people — slightly disproportionately young men — who perceive a lost future, not just a lost tool.

Entry-level jobs are collapsing first via anticipatory hiring freezes: organisations won't hire juniors for work 'AI will do soon', even though AI adoption is messy and the economic signal is muddied by the broader downturn.

Backlash is agency reclamation, not nostalgia: Gen Z's dumb-phone and offline-hobby trend echoes the hosts' own 'AI mish' concept, and 'human-made' art and music may gain value precisely because it proves a human did it.

The state response is chilling: after the Sam Altman attack, the FBI's 'anti-tech extremist' designation (from a thousand pages of leaked internal documents) risks sweeping peaceful protest — and even photographing a data centre — into 'pre-operational extremist planning'.

China is the counter-case: backlash there is 'dampened' rather than censored — the state lets sentiment surface enough to react, frames AI as national progress, and the job-loss pain hasn't landed yet; the global south may skip the backlash entirely because AI is levelling-up, not loss.

Jimmy's hypocrisy point cuts both ways: protesters are almost certainly using ChatGPT to organize, and everyone complaining about AI is already embedded in it — but he argues living in the system you criticize is legitimate.

jimmy: We're a few steps from the cliff edge, not over it — and the backlash may be partly an artifact of Western social media amplification; China shows what 'dampening' looks like.
The underlying grievance is real and structural: young people are worse off than their parents with no improvement in sight, so mass protest by end-2027 wouldn't surprise him.
He predicts an AI bubble pop between end-2026 and mid-2027, after which AI becomes significantly more expensive even as the world finds ways to cheapen it again.

On wealth concentration he sketches the Elysium scenario: the US as the space station in the sky, everyone else buying American AI labour — though the US backlash may be fiercest precisely because people there aren't okay with it either.
matt: He's been predicting mass social unrest since the podcast started and now believes we're on the cusp — Iraq-war-scale protests across the UK, US and Europe, with different groups protesting different harms.
The trigger is a terrifying realization: the AI revolution is top-down — no one voted for it, no one asked for it to happen this way, and it doesn't seem like anyone can stop it.
By end-2027 AI will be the number one electoral issue in developed countries, because voters will blame everything — including unrelated price shocks — on AI and big tech.
Governments will enact economically nonsensical youth employment schemes (e.g., paying young people to supervise AI) as a knee-jerk response, because doing nothing makes the unrest far worse.

title: FABLE BAN CONSPIRACIES, DATA CENTRES IN SPACE & APPLE'S AI FIGHTBACK: Jimmy & Matt debate their favourite AI stories from June 2026
description: Send us Fan Mail A top-tier AI model appears, gets jailbroken, and then disappears within 96 hours. From there, we get practical about why guardrails still feel so crude. We also talk about the commercial side: IPO pressure, circular financing, and why the race to outdo OpenAI can collide head-on with regulation. Then we widen the lens to the global response. Europe moves in the opposite direction with a renewed push for sovereign AI funding, and we discuss what “technological sovereignty” means when the US can cut off access overnight and open source models are catching up fast through model distillation.
